B1 / basement service floor

B1_LAUNDRY The laundry: WORS 1610 came from here

7.8 x 7.7 m west basement room off the public core (B1_LAUNDRY_DOOR); two washers, the airer, tubs / users: every household on its day; Teresa at 03:00 Saturday; Juno and her recorder on Thursdays / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Large bright room, brass flush-dome light, plain tan plaster walls, bare concrete floor with no drain.
  • Two wringer washers: grey box tubs on cream wooden stands with wooden-roller wringers on top; no motor, hose or drain.
  • Two grey rinse tubs on a wooden leg frame against a white-painted brick pier; no taps, supply pipes or waste.
  • Ceiling airer: wooden slat rack on ropes through pulleys, cleated to the pier; flat cream cloths hang from it.
  • Dark green Z-braced door on the far wall; furniture is spread thinly across a very large floor.
  • No baskets, soap, copper, mangle table, benches or wet marks on the floor.
  • Defect: Rinse tubs and washers have no water supply, taps or drains; no floor drain anywhere.
  • Defect: Hanging cloths are flat untextured rectangles.
  • Defect: Walls and floor show no damp, lime or soap staining in a wet room.

Interpretation

  • The set pieces are correct in type and read at a glance: wringers, tubs, airer.
  • Nothing is plumbed, so the room reads as a display rather than a wet basement laundry.
  • Scale is generous; the room would read fuller with the washers pulled toward the pier.

Narrative

Two galvanised wringer washers, the rinse tubs with their three draped cloths and the rope-and-pulley airer are installed and operate (WasherProp areas, the airer's lower/raise). The room should carry the building's week: a posted laundry schedule (Label3D) by the door with pencil tallies, a basket per household left under the airer with a chalked floor number, Mina's uniformly folded stack on the folding table, Lena's two extra households' loads, Evelyn's wiped-down machines, Omar's deep-service oil can and the bulb he changes. And the silence where a transmitter should be: a brass signal outlet high on the wall with a cloth lead that goes nowhere, painted over (Accord 11: one anchor painted over; Bible III). The player infers the most social room in the building, used by everyone and never at the same time, and the one thing in it that cannot be explained.

B1 / basement service floor

B1_PUBLIC_CORE Basement arrival: the stair foot and the reading nook

7.6 x 7.7 m core at the foot of the primary stair with the lift pit walls, doors to laundry and storage, the opening to the boiler approach; the reading nook with its emeralite lamp / users: everyone bound for the laundry; the reader in the nook / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Marble stair with iron balusters and wood rail; marble landing slab; upper flight reads as open-riser treads on a dark stringer.
  • Cool blue fill light on the walls and stair with no visible source; warm pool only from the hand lamp.
  • DT1: thin bright orange vertical streak at the wall-pier junction behind the stair (light leak).
  • Reading nook under a black steel lintel: red oriental rug, low desk with paper, metal bookshelf, green-shaded lamp lit.
  • TH is the closed B1_LAUNDRY_DOOR leaf filling the frame; no DT3 tile.
  • Floor is plain concrete; walls plain plaster; no basement signage, pipes or meters in frame.
  • Defect: Light leak: bright orange seam at the pier-wall junction in DT1.
  • Defect: Cool blue ambient on the core with no fixture to own it.
  • Defect: Upper stair flight shows daylight between treads (open risers) on a marble stair.

Interpretation

  • The nook is the only dressed moment on B1 and reads as someone's station; worth keeping.
  • Blue sourceless fill breaks the practical-light rule and makes 20:00 read as dusk.
  • Open-riser treads make a 1928 marble stair read mid-century.

Narrative

The stair arrives here under the fitted underside, beside the lift's basement landing. The reading nook (reading_nook.md: an original nook with the emeralite task lamp on its table) sits in the core; the basement floor plates point to laundry, workshop and boiler. The nook needs its reader's evidence: a book face down, a cold cup, a cushion; the stair foot needs the building's basement notices (boiler hours, the coal delivery date) and the mat where wet feet stop.

B1_BOILER_APPROACH The boiler approach

4.1 x 1.2 m lit retreat route from the core to the boiler room's fire door, with the shop door and the electrical recess off it / users: the player on the service round; Omar / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • 1.2 m corridor, plain tan plaster walls and concrete floor; no skirting, conduit or pipe runs along the walls.
  • Dark green-grey Z-braced metal doors with brass lever handles; fire door (DT2) closed and flush, rivet-dotted frames.
  • Galvanized duct drops from a square ceiling flange and elbows into the right wall above the open door (DT1); run terminates.
  • Public stair with marble treads and iron balusters visible at the corridor end (OV, DT3).
  • No corridor light fixture visible in any tile; only the hand-lamp pool lights the route.
  • Walls and floor show no wear, staining or scuffing along a service route.
  • Defect: No visible corridor light fixture despite the 'lit route' brief.
  • Defect: Corridor walls bare: no conduit, pipe run, skirting or wear on a plant-room approach.

Interpretation

  • Reads as a service passage; the duct and heavy doors say plant room ahead.
  • Without a fixture the 'lit retreat route' is lit only by the player; a cage lamp would sell it.
  • Door-and-duct vocabulary is period-plausible; the emptiness of the walls is the weak point.

Narrative

A 1.2 m corridor whose whole job is the retreat line from the firing door (ORISON_V2_BOILER_ACCESS). It should read as the one corridor built for a man carrying a shovel: a scuffed centreline, a coal-dust gradient toward the fire door, a fire bucket of sand on a hook, the breeching's heat showing on the plaster near the door.

B1 / basement service floor

B1_BOILER_ROOM The boiler room: the 1912 plant

6.15 x 9.5 m with the boiler on its grounded base, the water column, the breeching to the flue, the operating boiler-well window, doors to the coal room and the service stair / users: the player (firing, ash, draft, water column); Omar; Teresa's pre-shift patrol / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Cream jacketed boiler with dark horizontal bands on a dark plinth; flue rises to a galvanized ceiling duct with hanger rods.
  • Galvanized duct runs the ceiling to the right wall; a second elbow turns up into the ceiling at left.
  • Dark rectangle on the floor at the boiler foot (ash pit or grate); no fire door, shovel, ash cans or coal visible.
  • Free-standing plain cream partition wall beside the boiler; two dark doors; plain plaster walls, bare concrete floor.
  • DT2 (HandleReach) shows a four-pane glazed sash in a dark alcove with red-labelled items behind the glass.
  • DT1/DT3 boiler close-ups are nearly black; the lamp pool barely registers in this room.
  • No water column, gauge glass, pressure gauge or valve wheel readable in any tile.
  • Defect: Room has no visible light fixture and renders near-black in all three detail tiles.
  • Defect: Hand-fired coal boiler lacks fire door, ash door, shovel, ash cans and any coal within reach.
  • Defect: No gauge glass or water column visible for the 'water-column comparison' beat.
  • Defect: Flue and duct are plain galvanized sheet with no soot, rust or lagging.

Interpretation

  • The boiler reads as a sealed appliance, not a hand-fired coal plant: nothing to fire, rake or shovel.
  • Room is far darker than every other B1 space; the player cannot read the plant without a fixture.
  • The partition and glazed sash suggest an engineer's office or gauge window, but neither is legible.

Narrative

The boiler, its firing and ash doors, the draft damper, the water glass, the breeching and the well window are installed and operate; T01's neutral iron and restrained lagging are reviewed. The room should show the firing routine's evidence: the shovel leaning by the fire door, the ash can and its ring on the floor, the clinker rake, the coal-dust fan from the coal door, a chalked log on the wall by the water column (dates and levels as strokes), the oil can and rag by the damper. Light is the plant's own: the firebox glow when open, one cage bulb. The player infers a plant kept alive by hand for sixteen years.

B1 / basement service floor

B1_ELECTRICAL The electrical room: the fuse panel

4.1 x 4.3 m dry room south of the boiler approach with the fuse panel (G05) and its working front / users: the player (fuse repairs); Omar at 03:00 / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Small plain plaster room, bare concrete floor, brass flush-dome light blown out in DT2/DT3.
  • Fuse panel: small grey steel box with open door, brass knife switch, two porcelain plug fuses, red wire to a brass bus.
  • No conduit, service cable, meter or wiring enters or leaves the panel; black switch plate nearby.
  • Dark green Z-braced metal door on the far wall; a large flat dark-brown slab fills OV right (open leaf seen from inside?).
  • TH shows the room through the open door: panel, switch and dome light centred.
  • No shelves, spare fuses, rubber mat, warning sign or wear marks.
  • Defect: Fuse panel has no conduit or service entrance; every wire should terminate somewhere visible.
  • Defect: Large flat dark slab at OV right reads as an untextured plane (open door leaf back face?).
  • Defect: Two of three detail tiles show only the blown-out ceiling light.

Interpretation

  • The panel itself is well made and period-right; the room around it says nothing happened here.
  • A 'main panel room' with no incoming service reads as a prop on a wall.

Narrative

The fuse panel is implemented and reviewed (G05) and its maintenance activity works. The room should carry the 1912 wiring's stratigraphy: cloth-covered conductors on porcelain cleats along the wall to the panel, a later conduit run beside them (1928), a knife switch with a wooden handle, a shelf of fuse cartridges in a box, the chalk tallies Omar makes at 03:00, and the one thing a 1912 demonstration building would have: a brass signal distribution frame with a hundred cloth leads, labelled with blank tags, half of them to points nobody remembers (Bible VIII.3).

B1_ELECTRICAL_RECESS The electrical recess

1.8 x 1.0 m recess holding the panel-room leaf's outward swing off the boiler approach / users: nobody / coverage: partial

Observed

  • Four tiles only; OV and DT1 are the open dark green Z-braced door leaf at close range.
  • RV is a dark plaster corner with the door edge; TH shows the recess corridor to a closed Z-braced door.
  • Brass lever handle and rivet-dotted frame on the leaf; walls plain plaster, concrete floor.

  • The recess reads as a door swing pocket; nothing here tells a story beyond the door itself.

B1_MAINTENANCE_SHOP The maintenance shop: the player's bench

4.1 x 5.6 m opposite the electrical room with the repair bench, toolboard and parts shelf (b1_repair_bench, b1_toolboard, b1_parts_shelf), doors to the approach and the service stair / users: the player; Omar / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Wooden-top workbench on a black steel frame with a black bench vise and one drawer; good silhouette.
  • Toolboard: plywood panel with a hammer, four wrenches, a ring and small tools on pegs; flat but legible.
  • Parts shelf: bright silver-grey tubular uprights with orange wood shelves; holds two cream cubes and two grey speckled blocks.
  • Three tall plain wood boards stand upright against the right wall (OV), flat-topped.
  • Dark green Z-braced door; black switch plate with brass toggle; plain plaster walls, bare concrete floor.
  • Ceiling light blown out at frame top; no oil stains, sawdust, scrap or wear on the bench.
  • Defect: Parts shelving with bright zinc tube uprights reads post-1950 boltless shelving.
  • Defect: Shelf contents are untextured cream cubes and grey blocks.
  • Defect: Three vertical boards against the right wall have no visible purpose or texture detail.

Interpretation

  • Bench and toolboard sell 'repair shop' quickly; the shelf and its contents undercut the era.
  • The cubes and blocks read as placeholder parts rather than crates, tins or pipe fittings.

Narrative

The bench, toolboard and parts shelf are installed (the bench is a copy of Omar's). The shop should be the player's, not Omar's: the carried set's spare battery case on charge, a crate of capsules from HARDWARE PAINT, a vice, the bulb stock, a tally of the service round on the wall, and one broken household thing waiting (a toaster from 4A?). The toolboard's painted silhouettes with one hook empty (the ladder is HARDWARE PAINT's, not here). The player infers their own workplace and the super they share it with.

B1_COAL_ROOM The coal room: bunker, heap and the street chute

6.15 x 6.85 m annex off the boiler room with the bunker, fourteen coal-heap fixtures, the gravity chute to the closed street cover and its delivery aperture / users: the player; the coalman's delivery is static architecture / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Large bright room with a brass flush-dome ceiling light that blows out in DT1/DT3; plain plaster walls, clean concrete floor.
  • Coal heap is a dome of dark faceted lumps on a flat dark elliptical disc, about 2 m across, with a few scattered lumps.
  • Chute is a flat grey slab with one cream batten sloping from the upper corner; its lower end stops in mid-air short of the heap.
  • Dark green Z-braced metal door with brass handle; black switch plate on the wall (RV).
  • No coal dust, soot or staining on walls or floor; no bunker boards, shovel, barrow or sacks.
  • RV shows the chute's upper end as a boxy grey projection from the wall near the ceiling.
  • Defect: Chute lower end terminates in air about 0.5 m above the floor, not over the heap.
  • Defect: Coal heap sits on a flat dark disc base that reads as a decal.
  • Defect: Walls and floor spotless: no coal dust, no retaining boards, no tools.
  • Defect: Ceiling fixture blown out; two of three detail tiles are the lamp alone.

Interpretation

  • The room reads as an empty storeroom with a small pile dropped in it, not a working bunker.
  • A blown-out overhead light in a coal room removes the one place the hand lamp should matter.
  • The floating chute end tells the player the coal never arrived by chute.

Narrative

The bunker, heap and chute are installed (coal delivery progress). The room should show delivery and use: a coal shovel and the bunker's board gate, a dust fan from the chute's mouth, the heap's angle of repose with a shovel cut on the boiler side, a tally of deliveries chalked on the bunker board, a tin lamp on a nail (the only light besides the dome), and the hopper's rust. Earlier punchlist rows (untextured gray bin, no coal, no grime) were V1 and must be checked against the capture.

B1 / basement service floor

B1_RESIDENT_STORAGE Resident storage: eighteen bays

15.4 x 5.65 m with eighteen labelled bays (B1_STORAGE_BAYS) on central and east aisles, door from the public core / users: every household; Juno's tape boxes; the Transients' never-collected trunk / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Bays are tall pointed-top picket fences in orange-stained wood on both sides of a long aisle; white-painted brick wall at left.
  • Bay labels are Label3D text; '2C' (DT1) and '5B' (DT3) read mirrored from the back face; others read correctly.
  • Small white label glyphs hover at ceiling height along the aisle in OV/RV, detached from any post.
  • Every visible bay is empty: no trunks, crates, bicycles, furniture or padlocks.
  • Brass flush-dome light at the aisle end blows out in DT1/DT3; black switch plate on the wall (DT2).
  • TH: the storage door opens straight onto the public-core nook (rug, desk, lamp).
  • Defect: Bay labels mirrored when read from behind (2C, 5B) and floating as glyphs along the aisle.
  • Defect: All bays empty; no stored household goods anywhere.
  • Defect: Picket-fence partitions with pointed tops read as exterior garden fencing.
  • Defect: White brick wall and dome light blow out under the lamp.

Interpretation

  • Picket points read as a garden fence, not wire-mesh or lath cages with hasps.
  • Eighteen empty bays tell the player no resident has ever stored anything.
  • Mirrored and floating labels expose the lettering mechanism the Bible wants invisible.

Narrative

Eighteen bays with labels and nothing in them (the previous sweep's open finding: cage partitions solid, no doors, no contents was a V1 row to recheck). The bays should hold what eighteen households put in a basement in 1928: trunks, a bicycle (Cam's spare), a pram nobody has had a use for, Lena's bolts, Mae's crated objects under cloths, Omar's bay full of other people's broken things, Nadia's bay with rolled drawings, the Transients' bay with a trunk whose label has nine dates, and one bay padlocked and empty (2D's or 3C's). The player infers the building's attic, below ground, and reads each household twice.

B1 / basement service floor

B1_SERVICE_CORE Basement service core

3.7 x 6.2 m service stair continuation with doors to the boiler room and the shop / users: the player; Omar / coverage: inspected

Observed

  • Terrazzo floor with white chips reads well; marble treads, iron balusters with square feet, wood rail.
  • Upper flights read as open-riser treads on a dark stringer; soffits are flat dark planes.
  • Brass flush-dome at the stair ceiling; dark green Z-braced boiler-stair door with brass lever (DT3).
  • Plain plaster walls, no skirting, no handrail wear, no signage.
  • A tall marble slab face at the landing edge (OV right).
  • Defect: Open-riser treads on a marble stair read modern.
  • Defect: Service stair finished identically to the public stair; no wear, no painted dado.

Interpretation

  • Finish level matches the public stair; a service stair in marble and terrazzo reads a little grand.
  • Legible and bright; the player will not get lost here.

Narrative

The service stair's bottom: coal dust on the lowest treads, a bucket of sand, the floor plate. Nothing else.

BUILDING-WIDE / systemic findings and shared families

BW_BUILDING_WIDE Systemic findings that no single room can fix

Every floor; the evidence is the room sheets named in each change / users: every resident; the player / coverage: n/a (cross-cutting)

Observed

    Interpretation

      Narrative

      The room-by-room review repeats a small number of findings in dozens of rooms. They are listed once here with stable ids so the room pages can cite them instead of restating them, and so the implementing agent can fix a family rather than a room. In order of how much they cost the building's credibility: the six completion-interior homes are furnished with copied templates (1D carries a seamstress's furniture; 1A, 3D and 4D have only a bed, wardrobe, table and chair; 3D has no range); the three converted second bedrooms are not converted; several shared furniture variants read post-1950 (tulip-pedestal round tables, chrome wire shelving, square-steel-post shelves, slab-cushion sofas); bath tile is applied to both faces of bath walls so it shows in halls and bedrooms; ventilation ducts and their hangers end in air; the service spine is a bare block-out shell with no risers, lights or finishes; windows are bare of curtains and blinds everywhere at 20:00; bedding is flat slabs; shower curtains are rigid fluted cylinders; mirrors hang tilted off walls; cold cyan light leaks around door leaves and openings with no visible source; six homes have no radio; completion-interior main rooms are lit by flush domes where every authored living room has a pendant. None of these is a texture problem; they are variant, family and data problems, which is why they are cheap to fix once and expensive to fix per room.

      The 30 ft carriageway and both 15 ft walks between the Orison's front and the south block (Harukiya, gateway, kiosk), from the west hoarding to the east hoarding / users: everyone crossing; traffic / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • [route_orison_to_shop_bodega_0] View from the Orison door across the road: lit brick arch with a lattice gate at left.

      • [route_orison_to_shop_bodega_0] Defect: Flat untextured grey box buildings at right.

      • [route_orison_to_shop_bodega_1] Along the pavement past the Orison's brick flank; pink neon blade edge top-left; lamp post with a yellow lantern head mid-distance.
      • [route_orison_to_shop_bodega_1] Dark rectangle on the pavement at the building's base; kerb is a sharp cream edge over dark road.
      • [route_orison_to_shop_bodega_1] Across the road, a brick building with lit windows and one warm orange window; far buildings are dark flat blocks.

      • [route_orison_to_shop_bodega_2] Bodega corner: white fascia with red lettering DELI - GROCERY - OPEN 24 HOURS; the name line above is cut by the frame top.

      Interpretation

      • The walk from the Orison door to the bodega corner is legible: neon blade, lamp posts and the lit bodega fascia mark the route.
      • The storm is absent from every frame: clear starry sky with the Milky Way, dry road, no puddles or wet reflections.
      • Everything beyond the two facades is flat untextured blocking; pavements carry hard-edged dark rectangles that read as missing decals.
      • The bodega's bright printed OPEN 24 HOURS fascia and smooth green produce read modern, not 1927 second-hand.

      Narrative

      The route captures walk the north pavement from the Orison door to the bodega and back; the facade stations look at the building from the carriageway. The street works as built. At 20:00 in November it should also carry the block's trade and the day's paper: a newsstand's lit hatch (the News booth is in the Arcade; a second street kiosk is not proposed), an ash can at every areaway, horse consequence in the gutter with the restrained fly shimmer the commensals brief allows, the election's broadsides pasted on the hoarding, the laundry's steam vent on the Arcade's west flank (the Model Laundry is inside the Passage; its vent can still breathe onto the street), and sound: a train on the proposed viaduct, heard not seen (T-ENDS open question). The player infers a working Queens street that does not stop for the storm.

      Observed

      • [subway_approach] Across the road: brick building at left with a wide lit arch; inside it, a passage with a lattice grid and a lamp.

      • [subway_approach] Road is a flat black plane; sky black; right third of the frame nearly empty.

      Interpretation

      • The relationship reads: lit arcade arch at left, kiosk railings and glowing sign at right, two warm pools in a black field.
      • The lattice across the arch opening needs a closer station: from here it could read as a shuttered arcade.
      • With a dry black road the two lights do not connect; a wet surface would tie them together.

      Narrative

      A single approach station toward the kiosk. K0 and K1 are built: iron panels, wire glass, unlit EXIT / RAPID TRANSIT, eight treads, tiled cheeks, a finite dark terminus. In 1928 Queens the subway was the elevated along Roosevelt Avenue and the IND under construction; the kiosk's language is right. Nothing to add but sound and light: reflected train light up the stair and a draught, both listed as optional later gates.

Evidence of use (V5): worn thresholds and brass, a parcel shelf, ghost signs, one 1950s fluorescent retrofit in a cheap tenant (the dated-arrival phenomenon, like the jukebox records).       Narrative

      Terrazzo, wainscot, two benches, two windows with brick reveals, a noticeboard. Generous and empty. The lobby is the building's parliament and should show it: the noticeboard dense with notices (Nadia's memos signed Management, Evelyn's red-pencilled corrections, the laundry schedule, a lost-and-found card), the sealed Vantry master clock on the core wall four minutes fast with the time clock below it, the earliest photograph (1928) framed by the inner door, a radiator by the window with a dish of gloves drying on it, a bench with one end worn where the Transients wait facing the doors, a brass spittoon by the other, the lift annunciator's bell visible through the watch opening. The player infers a lobby that is used all day by eighteen people who disagree.

      F01_WATCH The watch room: detector, registers, tour key, annunciator

      4.2 x 4.4 m off the lobby opening with the ritual desk, the wire column, the watchman's detector clock, night register, signal register, tour key guard and the porter's call board; doors to the mail room and the core / users: the player (clock in, take the report); the night watch / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Watchman's clock: round dial in a wooden case (DT1); night register: wooden board with ledge, open book, sheet and hooks (DT2).
      • Signal register: wood-and-brass annunciator with coloured indicators and three dials; small key box beside it (DT3).
      • Porter's call board: narrow vertical panel with rows of small cells on the left wall.
      • Two block counters: a wood-grain box with sloped top and a plain flat-shaded cream box; a tall plain dark-olive cabinet.
      • Window to the lobby/street with night view; small desk with papers at RV lower right; dark Z-braced door.
      • Plain plaster walls, concrete floor, no fixture; lit only by the hand lamp.
      • Defect: Cream counter and dark-olive cabinet are flat-shaded primitives without edges or hardware.
      • Defect: No light fixture, chair or desk lamp at the watch station.

      Interpretation

      • The wall instruments are the best-made props on the floor and read as a watch station.
      • The counters and cabinet are untextured blocks that drag the room back to blockout.

      Narrative

      The smoke capture shows the instruments on bare plaster: the desk mass, the detector clock, the register shelf, the signal cabinet, the key guard, the annunciator with its row of flags, and a window to the lobby. G01-G03 are implemented and reviewed. The room needs its occupancy: the watchman's chair (the player's), a lamp on the desk, a coat on a hook, the tour route card on the wall (Label3D), a kettle on a gas ring, a cot folded against the wall (a night watch sleeps here between rounds), the wire column dressed with its terminal labels. The player infers the job: the building watched from this chair for sixteen years.

      F01_PUBLIC_CORE F01 public core: lift and stair

      The passenger lift's ground landing with the interlock (SR7-B), the primary stair and the openings to the lobby and the service transfer; the watch door beside the lift approach / users: all residents, the player, the lift / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Marble stair with iron balusters and wood rails; upper flights read open-riser on a dark stringer; cool white light from above.
      • RV: bright orange coarse-grain wainscot, an empty picture frame, a large framed opening/mirror showing a teal wall and lift door.
      • Brass plaque with partial engraved lettering beside a dark lift opening; lift car interior shows wainscot and patterned floor.
      • DT1-3 target OrisonV2Blockout, ServiceAlley and @Node3D@2335 and all show the same flat orange-tan plane.
      • BASEMENT signboard with smaller lines at the stair foot; yellow-and-white stripes under the stair (baluster shadows).
      • Dark brown door frame at TH left; marble landing soffits are flat planes.
      • Defect: Flat untextured orange-tan blockout plane visible at the stair foot.
      • Defect: Three detail tiles target blockout/node names, not fittings.
      • Defect: Cool sourceless white light flooding the stair hall.
      • Defect: Empty picture frame on the wall; wainscot wood grain scaled far too large.

      Interpretation

      • The lift and plaque are the forty-years-early beat and they read; the blockout face next to them does not.
      • Detail stations resolved to a blockout node, so the sheet's detail row is wasted.
      • Daylight-strength cool light at 20:00 contradicts the night.

      Narrative

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it. The lift landing is the building's most used square metre: the brass call plate, the dial, the gate rattle. The floor plate reads street/watch and service. Its unique piece: the lift inspection card. Cores carry sound up and down the building; this is where the Tenant's body is audible.

      F01 / 1A Evelyn Marsh

      F01_A_VESTIBULE Evelyn Marsh's vestibule

      Entry from the public hall; distributes to the main room and private hall / users: Evelyn Marsh / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Small vestibule with three cream panel doors converging; oak floor; black switch plate; brass handles.
      • Entry door (DT2): grey-green panel door with brass overhead closer, white peephole dot, brass handle.
      • Brown woven-texture strip runs across the bottom of the entry door leaf, like a mat applied to the door.
      • TH from the public corridor shows dark wood wainscot outside and the lit vestibule within.
      • No coat hooks, hall stand, mirror, umbrella stand or mat on the floor; five tiles only.
      • Defect: Mat-like woven strip textured onto the door's bottom rail.
      • Defect: No coat provision in a vestibule described as coats and distribution.

      Interpretation

      • Door hardware is good and period-plausible; the vestibule's 'coats' purpose is unsupported.

      Narrative

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. Evelyn Marsh should be legible here before any other room: a coat on a proper hanger, galoshes paired toe-out on a drip mat, a corrected shopping list pinned at eye height, an umbrella furled and buttoned. The entry opens straight off the lobby (F01_A_ENTRY_DOOR connects F01_LOBBY), so Evelyn's threshold is the most public threshold in the building: her door mat is the one the whole lobby sees, and it is the cleanest. Three doors (main, private hall, lobby) leave one wall for the landing set. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.

      F01 / 1A Evelyn Marsh

      F01_A_MAIN Evelyn's living room: the marking table and the properly laid tray

      7.45 x 3.35 m front room off the vestibule, one window to the street side, doors to the kitchen and the bedroom / users: Evelyn Marsh; the player on the Saturday bake round / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Long room: oak floor, cream walls, picture rail, cornice, baseboards, two brass flush-dome lights, cream panel doors.
      • Seven-column cast-iron radiator with brass valve and supply pipe under the window; reads well.
      • Sash window looks directly onto a red brick wall a metre or two away; a white disc (lamp reflection) sits on the glass.
      • One small dark table and one bentwood chair by the window; black toggle switch; nothing else in the room.
      • No rug, sofa, armchair, sideboard, pictures, clock, curtains or lamp.
      • Defect: Room almost empty: one table, one chair, one radiator in a long living room.
      • Defect: Window has no curtains and faces bare brick at close range.

      Interpretation

      • Reads as a corridor-shaped empty flat; 'living, meals and conversation' is not supported.
      • A retired teacher of pre-war order would have the most dressed room; this is the least.

      Narrative

      A long, narrow front room with one window. Today it holds a 5C-template table and chair and a radiator. It should hold a teacher's living room arranged in formal balance: the dining table set for one with a tray cloth and the good cup, the second cup on the dresser that nobody has used, a reading chair by the window with a floor lamp, a wireless on its table with the quiz programme she corrects aloud, and the two framed documents centred on the long wall as a pair. Everything is pre-war in cut and immaculate in keeping; the wear is the wear of thirty-one years of care, not of neglect: the chair arm polished by one hand, the table edge where the marking pencil rests, a rub on the floor where the chair is pulled out at exactly the same angle twice a day. The player should infer a woman who still keeps school hours for nobody, and who corrects the world because she cannot stop caring for it.

      Proposed backstory

      • The framed permission letter (1904) and the retirement certificate are the orderly pair.
      • The photograph on the wireless table is her husband, dead before the war.
      • The class register of 1954 is in the study with Peter Wren's name underlined.

      F01_A_KITCHEN Evelyn Marsh's kitchen

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Evelyn Marsh / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Cream enamel sink with ribbed drainboard and two brass taps on a grey angle-iron leg frame; black toggle switch above.
      • Tall cream cabinet with brass pull (icebox?) and, in TH, a cream cabinet topped by a dark-bronze dome with three copper rings.
      • No cooking range, oven or hob visible in any tile; no wall cupboard, table or chair.
      • Oak floor, cream walls, a horizontal moulding rail at about 1.5 m, flush-dome light; five tiles only.
      • A second shorter cream cabinet with a dark top at the far wall (TH); a thin shelf rail on the right wall.
      • Defect: No gas range or any cooking appliance visible.
      • Defect: Unidentified dark-bronze ringed dome on top of the cream cabinet.
      • Defect: No shelves, crockery, pans or dresser; walls bare.

      Interpretation

      • Washing is provided; cooking is not legible, so 'cooking and washing' is half a room.
      • The ringed bronze dome cannot be read as any 1927 appliance; it attracts the eye and explains nothing.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an electric monitor-top on splayed legs, new, expensive, noticeably loud, and the neighbours know who has one. What makes it Evelyn Marsh's is one place laid properly at every meal: a tray cloth, the good cup and the second cup that is never used, a tea caddy with a spoon on a string. The kitchen is compact (3.1 x 2.45 m) with the sink on a drainboard and the monitor-top she keeps immaculate; the hall opening lets the kettle be heard from the bath. The ice card convention does not apply: 1A is one of the four electric flats and the neighbours know it. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      F01_A_BATH Evelyn Marsh's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Evelyn Marsh / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • White brick-bond tile walls with dark grout, white hex mosaic floor, pedestal basin with black taps and trap, WC with dark wood seat.
      • Full-height fluted cream column from floor to ceiling in the corner with a moulded base and a black floor slot beside it.
      • Shower curtain (cream pleated) on a curved black rod in the far corner; no tub, tray or shower head visible beneath it.
      • Vent register: small cream box with a flat grey bracket plate near the ceiling (DT1).
      • Low cistern directly behind the WC bowl at seat height; black switch plate on tile; flush-dome light.
      • Five tiles only; no DT3.
      • Defect: Shower curtain hangs over bare floor: no tub, tray, waste or shower head.
      • Defect: Full-height fluted column in a bathroom reads as a scaled-up radiator or boxed riser.
      • Defect: Vent register box with flat grey plate reads as a placeholder.

      Interpretation

      • Tile and sanitaryware read period and clean; the column and curtain are the questions.
      • The curtain with nothing under it reads as a prop; the player expects a tub.
      • A low close-coupled cistern reads 1930s; a high tank with chain would sit better.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Evelyn Marsh's is a senior's medicated routine: the medicine cabinet is the full one, a glass with a dosing spoon on the basin, a bath rail she fitted herself and keeps polished. The bath rail is hers, not the landlord's: a brass rail screwed into the tile beside the receptor with the screw heads painted to match, the only thing in the flat she fitted herself. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      A square bedroom with a window, today a template bed and wardrobe.       F01_D_VESTIBULE Teresa Vale's vestibule

      Entry from the public hall; distributes to the main room and private hall / users: Teresa Vale / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Small oak-floored vestibule, cream walls, grey-green entry door with brass handle; black switch plate.
      • RV looks through to the main room: radiator with valve, window on brick, small table and two bentwood chairs.
      • TH from the corridor shows the lit flat beyond the open door; moon disc on the far window.
      • No coat hooks, mat, hall stand or mirror; walls bare.
      • Defect: No coat provision; bare walls.

      Interpretation

      • Clean and legible; coats are not provided here either.

      Narrative

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. Teresa Vale should be legible here before any other room: black laced shoes already pointing at the door, the navy cape on the first hook, a crushed cap, the thermos on the shelf where a hand finds it blind. 1D's entry is on the service hall (F01_D_ENTRY_DOOR connects F01_SERVICE_HALL), not the lobby: she leaves and returns by the back of the building at 22:00 and 07:40, past the staff restroom, and never sees the lobby crowd. The vestibule is 2.0 x 2.7 m with an opening to the main room; one wall only. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.

      F01_D_KITCHEN Teresa Vale's kitchen

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Teresa Vale / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Cream enamel gas range with black hob, four burners, splash back and glass-fronted oven door; blue-white glow on the hob.
      • Blue light spill on the wall cupboard underside and sink corner with no visible blue source.
      • Cream sink with ribbed drainboard on grey angle-iron legs; cream two-door wall cupboard; dark wood icebox with brass pull.
      • Soft dark smudges on the ceiling and upper wall corners near the cupboard and door (OV, RV).
      • Dark grey rectangular duct runs the ceiling and ends at the wall above the cupboard (TH, DT2).
      • Oak floor, cream walls, picture rail, baseboards; cream door with frosted panel; black switch plate.
      • Defect: Blue-white light on the range top and cupboard with no fixture to own it.
      • Defect: Dark shadow smudges on the ceiling and wall tops read as baked-lighting artefacts.
      • Defect: Range styling (glass oven door, splash back) reads a decade late for second-hand 1927.

      Interpretation

      • The best-provisioned kitchen on the floor: range, sink, icebox, cupboard all legible.
      • The blue glow reads as an electric hob or a light bug; a gas pilot would not light the room.
      • Glass-fronted oven and splash back push the range toward the 1930s.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it Teresa Vale's is a dented vacuum flask and a dull nickel kettle, one pan, a plate of yesterday under a cloth, the alarm clock silenced on top of the icebox. A B-type kitchen with its own door off the private hall. The alarm clock on the icebox top is the hero object: silenced, where she cannot hear it from bed. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      F01_D_BATH Teresa Vale's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Teresa Vale / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • White brick-bond tile, hex mosaic floor, pedestal basin with black taps, WC with dark wood seat and low cistern, cream panel door.
      • Full-height fluted cream column radiator in the corner (OV); sash window showing brick and a lit window outside.
      • Vent register (DT1): cream box on a grey duct that runs along the top of the tile wall and stops at the plaster corner.
      • Flush-dome light; black switch plate; lamp reflection halo on the window glass (DT2).
      • No tub, shower, towel rail, mirror, cabinet or hooks.
      • Defect: Grey duct run across the tile wall ends at the corner without a grille or wall penetration.
      • Defect: Full-height fluted column in a bathroom (same as 1A).
      • Defect: No tub or shower in a 'complete' sanitary room.

      Interpretation

      • Tile and fittings read as the same clean family as 1A; a nurse's bath would show a towel and a kit.
      • The exposed grey duct reads as a modern ventilation run bolted over tile.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Teresa Vale's is a night worker's bathroom used at the wrong hours: towel never fully dry, blackout against the light-slot, uniform collar soaking in the basin. The bath has a window (one of the few), so the blackout extends here: a towel pegged across it. The collar and cuffs soaking in the basin are the only white things in the room. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      F02_LANDING F02 passenger lift landing

      At the top of the primary stair's first flight; opening west to the west hall / users: all residents, the player, the lift / coverage: partial

      • OV and RV stations sit against plaster: orange lamp pool on a bare wall fills most of both tiles.

      • Exposed brick with a ledge beside a plastered corridor reads as an unfinished light-well, not a 1928 finish.
      • Teal spill behind the 2A door marks it as different; intentional or not, it draws the eye.

      Narrative

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it. The landing is the floor-and-unit decision for 2A and 2D; the lift's brass plate and dial are here. The punchlist asks each half-landing for its own piece; this landing's should be the first photograph the building owns (1928). Cores carry sound up and down the building; this is where the Tenant's body is audible.

      • No ceiling fixture, sconce or wall decoration visible; RV, TH and DT1 repeat the same 2A door framing.
      • Defect: Terrazzo chip scale reads as 8-10 cm pebbles rather than fine terrazzo.
      • Defect: Peephole renders as a flat white dot, not a brass fitting.
      • Defect: Exposed brick patch at the landing end of the hall.

      Interpretation

      • Reads as a convincing 1928 apartment-house corridor; wainscot, terrazzo and radiator carry the period.
      • The 2A door is clearly the destination; the approach from the stair is legible.
      • Brick at the landing junction breaks the plastered-hall language.

      Narrative

      A 1912 public corridor under 1928 paint: wainscot to 1.1 m, a dado rail, the picture rail that survived the demolition, enamel floor plates in both cores, a flush dome every few metres and the apartment doors with their transoms. This is the first apartment approach the player walks on the first shift: Mina's door with its transom and a mat squared to the millimetre; the only hall in the building with a milk bottle rinsed and inverted. Nothing else should distract from the door. The halls are where neighbours meet and where the building's own voice is loudest: a riser knocks, a door spills light, the lift gate rattles in the shaft.

      F02_A_VESTIBULE Mina Vale's vestibule

      Entry from the public hall; distributes to the main room and private hall / users: Mina Vale / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Small vestibule: oak strip floor, cream plaster, white baseboard, tan two-panel entry door with brass lever.
      • RV: black push-button switch plate on the wall; living room beyond with desk, chair and wire shelves.
      • RV: a resident in a dark suit stands by the shelves in the living room.
      • TH: door open on brass hinges; view through to a lit pendant, wire shelves and a window.
      • No coat hooks, hall stand, mirror, rug or labels; walls bare.
      • DT1 duplicates OV; DT2 shows the door leaf and a dark threshold saddle.
      • Defect: No coat storage or hall furniture despite the 'privacy and distribution' role.

      Interpretation

      • Functions as a doorway, not a room; nothing in it says who lives here.
      • For a resident who labels everything, the absence of any hook or label is a missed character beat.

      Narrative

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. Mina Vale should be legible here before any other room: a key board with every hook labelled, a numbered coat hook strip, a wall file of out-letters, a label on the label maker's box. A 1.95 x 2.7 m vestibule opening straight into the main room. Mina's landing set is a key board with every hook labelled and a numbered coat strip; the labels are blank card rectangles at this scale (no lettering), but the regularity reads from the door. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.

      F02 / 2A Mina Vale (Case 01)

      F02_A_MAIN Mina's living room: the working wall

      8.1 x 6.95 m, two west windows, openings to the vestibule and kitchen, door to the private hall / users: Mina Vale; the player for the whole of Case 01 / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Large living room: oak floor, cream plaster, picture rail, cornice, lit conical pendant, two bare windows.
      • Round dining table on a white flared pedestal base; two bentwood chairs; boxy pale grey sofa with slab cushions.
      • Two chrome wire shelving units with plain grey and white boxes; cream film projector with two reels on a desk.
      • Flat teal box about 0.5 m on a small side table; dark console cabinet by the kitchen door; dark half-bowl mounted on the wall.
      • DT3: wireless table with a black flat set and a glowing white sphere lamp; push-button switch above.
      • DT2: low dark coffee table carrying a black tray with three round items.
      • Resident: woman in grey suit and cloche hat standing mid-room (OV); dark figure by the shelves (RV).
      • Defect: Dining table pedestal (white flared tulip base) reads post-1955.
      • Defect: Sofa is a boxy slab form with no rolled arms or tufting; reads modern.
      • Defect: Wire shelving renders as bright chrome; reads post-1950.
      • Defect: Flat teal box on the side table has no visible texture or detail.
      • Defect: Dark half-bowl object mounted on the wall near the kitchen door, unexplained.
      • Defect: Windows have no curtains, shades or blinds at 20:00.

      Interpretation

      • Reads as a working caption editor's flat: projector, desk, shelves of boxes; the story is legible.
      • The tulip-base table and slab sofa pull the room toward the 1950s-60s and fight the 1927 second-hand rule.
      • Bare windows and an unexplained wall bowl read unfinished rather than lived-in.

      Narrative

      The largest living room in the building and the one the player studies longest. Today it holds a sofa, three wire shelving units, a round table and two chairs, a coffee table with the deck, a wireless table and radio, a projector on a stand, the repaired bookshelf and the radiator; Mina stands in it at 20:00. The walls are bare. The decor profile asks for a working wall: captions visible from the desk, images arranged so that one confrontational axis runs from the desk to the thing she never annotated. The desk is in the bedroom (right for her), so this room is the public face of her discipline: the shelves hold labelled boxes in rows with their labels facing out, every cable runs to a point and is tied, the sofa has one cushion squared and one with a dent, the coffee table carries the deck and a labelled jar of pencils; the unlabelled box sits in plain sight on the lowest shelf with its blank face forward. The player infers a woman who has annotated her whole life except one object, and that the object is the point.

      Proposed backstory

      • The blank card on the caption wall is the four seconds.
      • The unlabelled box holds the stenotype paper of one afternoon in court.

      F02_A_KITCHEN Mina Vale's kitchen

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Mina Vale / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak strip floor, cream plaster with a trim band, white two-door wall cupboard mounted high, window with a white disc outside.
      • Cream enamel gas range on legs with four black burners, oven door and chrome-trimmed handle.
      • White refrigerator with a dark cylindrical compressor stack on top (monitor-top type) on slim legs.
      • Grey slab sink on thin legs with wire dish rack, plates and a white cup; small enamel-top table with a kettle.
      • RV: white counter cabinet at left with a dark flat object on top; open doorway to the living room.
      • Counters otherwise empty: no jars, pans, food, towels or shelves.
      • Defect: Wall cupboard is a plain white box with no visible handles or trim.
      • Defect: Sink reads as a grey untextured slab on tube legs.
      • Defect: Oak strip floor in a kitchen; linoleum or tile expected for 1928.
      • Defect: Bright white disc outside the window is a flat circle with no falloff.

      Interpretation

      • Monitor-top fridge and enamel range read correctly as 1927 kitchen equipment; the room is legible as a kitchen.
      • Sparse surfaces make it a showroom rather than a lived-in flat.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an electric monitor-top on splayed legs, new, expensive, noticeably loud, and the neighbours know who has one. What makes it Mina Vale's is labelled jars in rows, a kitchen scale, a measured half-loaf, the icebox shelves labelled in her own hand. Mina's kitchen carries the Case 01 refrigerator caption residue after the first wake; the fridge is a monitor-top in data where the Bible allows four electric flats (1A, 3A, 5B, 6C). Converting it to an icebox keeps the caption marker (it binds to the refrigerator marker, not the model). Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      F02_A_BATH Mina Vale's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Mina Vale / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • White subway tile walls to ceiling, white hex mosaic floor, lit flush-dome light, dark vent grille high on the wall.
      • Pedestal lavatory with fluted column, black taps and exposed black trap; framed mirror above tilted forward off the wall.
      • Toilet with dark wood seat, low white tank, wall paper holder with roll; black push-button switch plate.
      • Cream shower curtain hangs as a rigid pleated cylinder on a curved black rod; tub not visible behind it.
      • No towel, soap, bath mat or toiletries.
      • Defect: Mirror hangs tilted about 15 degrees, top edge away from the tile.
      • Defect: Shower curtain is a rigid fluted cylinder with no drape or hem.
      • Defect: Lamp pool blows the sink-wall tile out to near white.

      Interpretation

      • Reads as a correct 1928 white-tile bath; the fixtures carry the period.
      • Bare of use: the player sees a bath nobody has washed in.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Mina Vale's is a single adult who keeps things exact: one toothbrush, one glass, towel squared on the rail, nothing on the floor. The smoke capture shows the standard set: pedestal basin, WC, curtain, cabinet, register. For Mina add only exactness: the toothbrush parallel to the basin edge, the towel's fold aligned to the rail end. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      The desk, its chair, the pinboard, the green office lamp, the papers, the mug and the headphones are all here, with the bed, nightstand and wardrobe. The room should read as two rooms sharing a wall: the desk side exact, lit by the lamp, the pinboard dense with cards; the bed side dark, the slate suit on the wardrobe door for the morning that will start at 13:30.       Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Lena Ortiz / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak floor, cream plaster with trim band, white two-door wall cupboard, lit flush dome, half-glazed white door.
      • Dark oak icebox with brass hinges and latch; cream enamel gas range with one burner lit blue and no pot.
      • Cream enamel sink with brass taps on a grey slab support with grey legs; wire dish rack with plates and a cup.
      • Cream two-door floor cupboard at right; black push-button switch plates.
      • No pans, jars, food, towels or shelves; surfaces otherwise empty.
      • Defect: Gas burner lit with nothing on it; blue glow strong in every tile.
      • Defect: Sink support is a flat grey untextured slab and legs.
      • Defect: Wall cupboard is a plain white box with slot handles.

      Interpretation

      • Icebox, range and enamel sink read correctly as 1928; the most convincing kitchen on the floor.
      • A burner left burning with no pot reads as an oversight unless scripted.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it Lena Ortiz's is the biggest pots in the building, a stack of borrowed plates with other people's names chalked underneath, a pie dish wrapped to go. The B-type kitchen with its own door: the biggest pots in the building on the range, a stack of borrowed plates chalked underneath, a pie dish wrapped to go for the Ortiz dinner on Sunday. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      F02_B_BATH Lena Ortiz's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Lena Ortiz / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • White subway tile walls, hex mosaic floor, lit flush dome, dark vent grille high on the wall, bare window with white sill.
      • Pedestal lavatory with fluted column, black taps and trap; framed mirror beside the window tilted forward.
      • Toilet with dark wood seat and lid raised, low white tank; cream pleated curtain cylinder on a black rod.
      • Grey vertical strips run up the tile corners.
      • Hex floor texture shows wavy ripple distortions across the floor.
      • No towel, soap, mat or toiletries.
      • Defect: Hex floor texture ripples and warps visibly (OV, RV, DT3).
      • Defect: Mirror tilted off the wall.
      • Defect: Curtain is a rigid fluted cylinder.
      • Defect: Grey untextured vertical strips at tile corners.

      Interpretation

      • Period-correct fixtures; reads as the same bath kit as 2A.
      • Rippled floor and the rigid curtain read as asset issues, not decay.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Lena Ortiz's is a single adult's ordinary use: one of everything, a second towel that is really a floorcloth. The bath has a window; a darned stocking dries on the rail (wardrobe bible: one darned at the heel). The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. Juno Kells should be legible here before any other room: cable cases stacked against the wall, a man's ulster on the hook, headphones hung by the cable, takeout menus under a magnet on the door. 2C's entry opens directly off the public core, so the cable cases stacked inside the door are heard being dragged across the landing at 02:00. The ulster on the hook is a man's.       Observed

      • Small room: oak floor, cream plaster, cornice; two identical light-oak two-door wardrobes side by side against the far wall.

      • Reads as a closet, not a 'household work and storage' studio.

      Narrative

      A windowless closet with two wardrobes, authored as household work and storage. For Juno it is the stolen session archive (hero object): one wardrobe keeps clothes, the other is shelved and full of tape boxes dated in her hand, with one reel box labelled only with a 1927 date. The player who opens the second wardrobe sees an archive, not a wardrobe.

      Proposed backstory

      • One reel box labelled only with a 1927 date.

      F02 / 2C Juno Kells (case)

      F02_C_BATH Juno Kells's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Juno Kells / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • White subway tile, hex mosaic floor with ripple distortion, lit flush dome, cream two-panel door.
      • Rectangular sheet-metal duct under the ceiling on three hanger rods with a louvred grille (DT1).
      • Toilet with dark wood seat up, low white tank, paper holder; pedestal lavatory with fluted column and black taps.
      • Cream pleated curtain cylinder on a black rod; tub not visible.
      • Door wall is plain plaster where the rest is tile (DT2).
      • No towel, soap, mat or toiletries.
      • Defect: Sheet-metal duct with hanger rods under the ceiling reads post-period.
      • Defect: Hex floor texture ripples.
      • Defect: Curtain is a rigid fluted cylinder.

      Interpretation

      • Same bath kit as 2A/2B; the exposed duct is the only distinct element and reads industrial rather than 1928.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Juno Kells's is a single adult's ordinary use: one of everything, a second towel that is really a floorcloth. Yesterday's kohl on the basin edge; a silver ear cuff on the shelf (wardrobe bible). The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      Narrative

      The smoke capture (teleported) shows a bare, lit shell: oak floor, plaster, a ventilation duct with its hangers along the ceiling, a radiator riser, one bath register. What the player should infer, from the hall only, is that someone pays attention to this door: the Bible's own silence (VIII.5.h) applied to one address.

      F03_PUBLIC_CORE F03 public core: stair, lift and 3C's locked door

      The dog-leg stair and lift at the centre; 3C's locked entry (F03_C_ENTRY_DOOR) opens here; openings to the east and west halls / users: all residents, the player, the lift / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Marble-tread stair with black iron balusters and oak handrail; cream textured plaster; marble stringer; period-credible.
      • No lift door, cage or indicator visible in any of the four tiles despite the 'passenger lift' caption.
      • RV: upper flight's marble treads carry sky-blue reflection patches, reading as daylight at 20:00.
      • TH: brass floor plaque with lettering on the wall; oak wainscot panel is a flat veneer sheet without stiles or rails.
      • TH: two small dark triangular shapes at the ceiling line near the plaque; unidentified, possibly clipped geometry.
      • DT1: 3C entry door closed, cream two-panel leaf, brass knob, oak saddle; lamp pool on the leaf.
      • No ceiling fixture visible; stairwell is evenly bright with no visible practical source.

      • Defect: Two unidentified dark wedges at the ceiling beside the floor plaque (TH)
      • Defect: Wainscot panel is a flat continuous veneer sheet with no panel divisions
      • Defect: Lift not present in frame; its dressing cannot be verified

      Interpretation

      • The stair reads as a 1920s apartment-house core; the player would accept it without question.
      • With the lift absent the core's 'transfer' function cannot be read from these frames.
      • Blue-tinted marble above breaks the November-night read; it suggests a sky probe leaking into reflections.

      Narrative

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it. The core on this floor carries the second sealed door; Omar collars residents here between 19:00 and 21:00 (schedule: overflow). The half-landing above is Jonah's pause (schedule 17:00). Cores carry sound up and down the building; this is where the Tenant's body is audible.

      F03_EAST_HALL F03 east hall: the approach to Omar

      From the core east to the service crossing / users: Omar, whoever has collared him / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Long corridor: oak wainscot both sides, cream textured plaster, cream terrazzo floor with grid pattern; one small framed picture.
      • Wainscot is a continuous flat wood-grain sheet with no stiles, rails or cap mouldings; grain scale large.

      Interpretation

      • Reads as a decent 1920s apartment corridor at a glance; the flat veneer wainscot weakens it up close.
      • The blue plane at the core end reads as placeholder, probably the lift front; the player would notice it.
      • Light without a source reads as a studio, not a hallway at 20:00.

      Narrative

      A 1912 public corridor under 1928 paint: wainscot to 1.1 m, a dado rail, the picture rail that survived the demolition, enamel floor plates in both cores, a flush dome every few metres and the apartment doors with their transoms. A hall where things wait for the super: a radiator section on the floor against the wall, a labelled parts bag hung on the dado, a crate of somebody's broken lamp. Nothing in the route. The halls are where neighbours meet and where the building's own voice is loudest: a riser knocks, a door spills light, the lift gate rattles in the shaft.

      Narrative

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. Malcolm Reed should be legible here before any other room: a boot scraper, hobnailed boots on newspaper, a trug, soil tracked in a fan from the mat, a flat cap on a nail. A 1.95 x 2.7 m vestibule off the west hall: boot scraper, hobnailed boots on newspaper, a trug, the flat cap on a nail, and soil in a fan from the mat that fades toward the main room. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.

      Narrative

      The potting bench, the specimen, the cuttings and seed jars, the radio and the repaired bookshelf are installed. The room should be a botanical study (decor profile): the propagation shelf across both west windows at sill height, cuttings in reused jars in rows with their dates on tags, the bench with a watering tray, soil sweepings, a trug and the secateurs' sheath; the dining table pushed to the wall and used for repotting; the propagation diagram and the cutting portrait on the wall as evidence, not decor; and one shelf spot clear and dusted. The player infers a man who keeps other people's plants alive and one plant alive against a goodbye.

      • The gap on the shelf is where the plant would have been happiest.

      F03_A_KITCHEN Malcolm Reed's kitchen

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Malcolm Reed / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Cream enamel gas range; GE monitor-top electric fridge, cream cabinet with black coil top; both read right for 3A.
      • Washing is a grey-topped table with a dish rack, plates and a chrome-looking kettle; taps not clearly visible.
      • White base cabinet with speckled laminate-look top and a black electric toaster with cord.
      • Upper cupboard is a plain white flat box with two doors; no moulding.

      • OV left edge: flat olive-cream slab close to the camera (door leaf or pier).
      • No ceiling fixture visible.

      • Defect: Flat white upper cupboard and speckled counter read mid-century
      • Defect: Black toaster reads modern; should be nickel

      Interpretation

      • Monitor-top and range tell the story; the cabinetwork reads later than 1928.
      • Without a visible sink and taps the 'washing' half of the caption is unreadable.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an electric monitor-top on splayed legs, new, expensive, noticeably loud, and the neighbours know who has one. What makes it Malcolm Reed's is jars not tins, a compost pail under the sink, seed trays on the sill, the empty memorial pot above the sink holding soil and nothing. One of the four electric flats: the monitor-top is correct and loud. The empty memorial pot sits on the sill above the sink holding soil and nothing; the compost pail is under the sink; jars, not tins, on the cupboard shelf. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Malcolm Reed's is a single adult's ordinary use: one of everything, a second towel that is really a floorcloth. Soil in the basin trap, a nail brush, hands that never come clean (wardrobe bible); the punchlist's F03_A_BATH toilet-in-shower overlap was a V1 row and must be rechecked in the capture. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      Interpretation

      • The room reads clearly as a repair technician's living space; the bench and board carry the story.
      • Tulip table and grey steel rack read mid-century, breaking the 1927 second-hand rule.
      • Untextured grey bins and the flat bench carcass read as placeholders up close.

      Narrative

      The workbench, two tool shelves, toolboard, parts crate, trays, jars, manuals, coil, the friction bench lamp, the wall radio and the projector are installed; the room is already the most specific in data. The logic the lived-in brief asks for is intake on one side, outgoing on the other, the bench between, and a clear service aisle: a crate by the door labelled with tags for things waiting diagnosis (story panel), a shelf of repaired things wrapped and tagged for return, and on newspaper on the floor the sacrificial teardown: a radio chassis half dismantled with its screws in a saucer, kept that way. Two of every appliance. The player infers a man who repairs everyone's things, keeps one broken for company, and whose home is maintained to a degree nobody else's is.

      Proposed backstory

      • The teardown is a radio chassis from the night of the 1977 blackout.

      F03_B_KITCHEN Omar Bell's kitchen

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Omar Bell / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Cream enamel gas range with black top; dark oak icebox with brass hardware (labelled FRIDGE_01); both read period.
      • Service door is a flat charcoal speckled slab with brass knob and peephole dot; no panels, rails or rivets.
      • White base cabinet with speckled laminate-looking top; black electric toaster-like box with glowing grille and cord.
      • Upper cabinets are plain white flat boxes with dark gap lines; no mouldings or glazing.
      • Sink is a small wall-hung cream basin on a bracket with a plate in it; no drainboard or legs.
      • Cream dish shelf with plates; cream walls with painted dado line; oak floor; black switch plate.
      • No ceiling fixture visible; room bright.
      • Defect: Flat-front white upper cabinets read mid-century
      • Defect: Service door is a featureless charcoal slab
      • Defect: Black toaster-like appliance with glowing grille reads modern
      • Defect: Speckled laminate-look counter top on the base cabinet
      • Defect: Kitchen sink undersized for 1928; no drainboard or legs

      Interpretation

      • Range and icebox sell 1928; the cabinets and door pull it toward the 1950s.
      • The slab service door could be a kalamein door but has nothing to read as metal-clad.
      • The toaster is signal-less so should be nickel and Bakelite, not black.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it Omar Bell's is two of every appliance, one working and one half torn down on newspaper with its screws in a saucer; a lid gasket replaced, labelled with the date. The only kitchen with a service door onto the spine (F03_B_SERVICE_DOOR): a workshop-enamel range (Appliance Bible IV: masking-tape residue, marker numbering, one panel replaced in mismatched paint) and a lid gasket replaced and dated. The kitchen linear light is his own fitting. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. Rhea Sato should be legible here before any other room: a dressing mirror turned to the door, a hat stand with three cloches, a scarf over the mirror corner, a shoe tree. A 2.6 x 2.7 m vestibule with three doors (entry, main, private hall): the dressing mirror turned to the door, a hat stand with three cloches, a shoe tree. The A-type plan gives her a proper entrance and she uses it as a stage wing. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an electric monitor-top on splayed legs, new, expensive, noticeably loud, and the neighbours know who has one. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Rhea Sato's is a singer's throat routine: steam kettle on the floor, a jar of pastilles, a mentholated inhaler, two glasses (gargle and rinse). A singer's bathroom: the steam kettle, pastilles, an inhaler, two glasses. The punchlist's magenta hamper intersecting a tan box was a V1 row; recheck. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it.       • The best-reading public corridor on the floor; proportions and finishes are period-credible.
      • The 4B transom label makes the player's door legible from the landing.
      • Brick at the landing junction breaks the plaster-and-wainscot language.

      Narrative

      A 1912 public corridor under 1928 paint: wainscot to 1.1 m, a dado rail, the picture rail that survived the demolition, enamel floor plates in both cores, a flush dome every few metres and the apartment doors with their transoms. The hall the player walks most. Its threshold evidence is the player's own: a service slip under the door, a boot scuff at the jamb. Noel's Sunday coffees happen at 4C's door on the core, not here. The halls are where neighbours meet and where the building's own voice is loudest: a riser knocks, a door spills light, the lift gate rattles in the shaft.

      Narrative

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it. 4C's door on the core is where the brothers drink their coffee on Sunday (schedule: the door opens at noon); Cam's bicycle wheel marks the wall beside it. Cores carry sound up and down the building; this is where the Tenant's body is audible.

      F04_A_VESTIBULE Peter Wren's vestibule

      Entry from the public hall; distributes to the main room and private hall / users: Peter Wren / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak floor, cream plaster, khaki two-panel hall door with brass knob, white frame; black push-button switch plate.
      • Sheet caption reads '2B privacy, coat storage and distribution' on a 4A sheet.
      • No coat hooks, stand, mirror, mat or fixture; walls bare.
      • RV: main room beyond with round pedestal table, bentwood chairs, cast-iron radiator under a dark window, and a dark unlit opening.
      • TH: the hall side is dark navy-black with the door leaf open, brass hinges visible.
      • Lamp pool blows out the near plaster.
      • Defect: No coat storage.
      • Defect: Caption names 2B.
      • Defect: Bare walls; lamp blow-out.

      Interpretation

      • Coat storage is the vestibule's stated purpose and nothing provides it.
      • The caption unit mismatch suggests the station set was copied from 2B.

      Narrative

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. Peter Wren should be legible here before any other room: an umbrella in a drip tray that has overflowed into a tide mark, brown Oxfords with the heel worn on the outside, a hat a size out on the shelf, a stamped envelope not yet posted. 2.0 x 2.7 m off the service crossing: the umbrella in its drip tray with a tide mark on the floor, Oxfords with the heel worn outside, a derby a size out on the shelf, a stamped envelope not yet posted. The grid starts here: everything square to the wall. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.
