      F04_A_MAIN Peter's living room: the measured grid

      4.15 x 4.5 m, one window, openings to the vestibule and the private hall / users: Peter Wren (20:00: FORMS, his own affairs by post) / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak floor, cream plaster with picture rail, lit drum pendant; cast-iron radiator with valve under an uncurtained window with brick and a white disc.
      • Round dining table on a white flared tulip pedestal with three bentwood hoop-back chairs.
      • Plain writing table with square legs, one sheet of paper, a white-shaded desk lamp (RV); a bentwood chair.
      • Dark glass-fronted barrister bookcase with books (DT2, DT3).
      • Wireless table: small dark table with a dark upright panel and a white curved shape; not readable as a radio.
      • A flat white door leaf stands open at the hall opening; walls bare; no rug, pictures or curtains.
      • Defect: Tulip pedestal dining table.
      • Defect: Radio not legible.
      • Defect: Bare walls, no curtains or rug.
      • Defect: Blown-out white disc in the window.

      Interpretation

      • The legal clerk's room has the right inventory but the tulip base is a 1950s form in a 1927 flat.
      • Exact and rumpled is not shown: one sheet on the desk and nothing else of Wren.
      • The radio needs a readable cabinet or horn; at present it is an abstract pair of shapes.

      Narrative

      The writing table, the round dining table and two chairs, the wireless table and radio, the sectional bookshelf and the story briefs are installed. The room should be a measured grid: the writing table square to the window with document stacks staged by status (in, pending, re-check) each under a brass weight, the date stamp and ink pad aligned to the blotter edge, municipal binders in a row with their spines flush, the two framed pieces (submission and uncertainty) hung on one centreline almost too carefully (decor profile), a drip tray under the radiator valve, and at this station too an unresolved form 11-B, face up. The player infers a man who files to avoid deciding, and that the grid is the deciding he can do.

      Proposed backstory

      • Every unresolved form is form 11-B at a different stage.

      F04_A_KITCHEN Peter Wren's kitchen

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Peter Wren / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak floor, cream plaster with a moulded rail; no window and no exhaust or vent visible despite the wet-stack caption.
      • Tan enamel range with black top, ring burners, oven window, short black legs; backsplash panel.

      • Function is complete; period reads through the icebox, sink stand and range, undercut by the flat white cabinets.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it Peter Wren's is identical tins in identical rows, five identical lunch pails, a toaster with a replacement form taped to it that was never filed. Identical tins in identical rows on the wall cupboard shelf; five identical lunch pails; the toaster with a replacement form taped to its side (a blank form rectangle, never filed). Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      F04_A_BATH Peter Wren's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Peter Wren / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Subway tile walls, hex mosaic floor with a mottled grey wear pattern, plaster above the tile line; blown-out flush dome.
      • WC in the corner: white bowl and dark wooden seat with lid raised; no cistern, tank or flush pipe visible in any tile.
      • Pedestal sink with brass taps and exposed trap; angled dark-framed mirror cabinet above.
      • Shower: cream pleated curtain hanging closed as a fluted cylinder from a ring; no tub or tray visible.
      • Sash window high on the wall with brick and a bright disc; louvered vent box above it; grey vertical tile strip at the corner.
      • Black switch plate on the plaster; khaki two-panel door.
      • Defect: WC has no cistern.
      • Defect: Shower curtain reads as a fluted column.
      • Defect: No tub.
      • Defect: Orange lamp cast over white tile.

      Interpretation

      • A WC without a cistern cannot work; it breaks the every-pipe-terminates rule.
      • The closed pleated curtain reads as a column, not a curtain; half-drawn it would read.
      • Captioned complete, but there is no tub.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Peter Wren's is a single adult who keeps things exact: one toothbrush, one glass, towel squared on the rail, nothing on the floor. A bath with a window; a celluloid collar drying on the rail; a form 11-B on the cistern lid (the bathroom station). The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      Narrative

      The vestibule is the first room the player reads and the one that decides whether the flat belongs to somebody. the player should be legible here before any other room: a service cap, the maintenance keyring on a nail, a stack of printed slips under a brass weight, the drip of the carried set's battery case on the mat. The punchlist names this one of the only two undressed rooms in the building (0.54 records per square metre median; here zero). The operator's landing set: a service cap, the maintenance keyring on a nail, printed slips under a brass weight, a drip on the mat from the carried set's battery case. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.

The drop-octagon clock on the wall where the desk chair can see it (it must be wound; hold E). The punchlist's featureless white box must be identified in the capture.       • Flush ceiling fixture lit (TH); black object with a short cord on the counter at OV left.
      • Round pedestal dining table seen through the opening in RV.
      • Defect: Range burners read as electric coils; range sides carry a wood-grain material.
      • Defect: White flat base cabinets with stone tops read modern.
      • Defect: Oak floor in the kitchen.
      • Defect: Blown-out white disc in the window.

      Interpretation

      • The icebox and sink stand are the period anchors; the base cabinets and burner rings pull toward 1950.
      • Oak flooring in a wet room reads wrong for a tenement kitchen; linoleum or tile expected.
      • Complete in function but unworn: no utensils, stains, shelves or crockery beyond one plate.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it the player's is a kettle and a toaster on a counter otherwise bare, a tin of biscuits, the landlord's portable fan, slips and carbons under the bread board. The kettle and toaster on a counter otherwise bare; the landlord's portable fan on the floor by the opening (box fan, OPERATE); a tin of biscuits; the C1 roach scatter at the switch is landed and must stay. A trash can is one of the 4B semantic requirements. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      F04_B_BATH the player's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: the player / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • White subway tile walls with dark grout, white hex mosaic floor, cream plaster ceiling; a blown-out flush dome.
      • Pedestal sink with brass taps and exposed trap; WC with dark wooden seat and white close-coupled low tank.
      • White column radiator by the door; tub edge visible at RV lower right; beige shower curtain on a dark rod.
      • Frosted sash window with a bright disc; a louvered vent box above the window (DT1).
      • Dark-framed mirror cabinet at upper left (OV, DT2); black switch plate by the door.
      • Whole room washed yellow-orange by the lamp; tile and fixtures lose their white.
      • Defect: Lamp colour cast turns white tile orange.
      • Defect: Louvered vent box sits on the tile face rather than in it.
      • Defect: Close-coupled tank reads later than 1928.
      • Defect: Tub barely captured by any station.

      Interpretation

      • The best-provisioned bath on the floor: every fixture a 1928 bath needs is present.
      • The orange cast hides the tile and makes the room read dirty rather than worn.
      • The vent box reads as a bolted-on grille rather than a wall register.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one the player's is a single adult's ordinary use: one of everything, a second towel that is really a floorcloth. A window bath; the player's own: a razor, a tin of tooth powder, the towel never squared. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Cam Ortiz and Noel Price / coverage: inspected

      • Oak floor, plaster with picture rail; one wall is full-height white subway tile beside the sink.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it Cam Ortiz and Noel Price's is one side of the counter quick food in paper, the other side preserved and labelled; a dead icebox nobody empties; a battered copper kettle both use. One kitchen, two centuries: Cam's side quick food in paper, Noel's side preserved and labelled; the icebox is dead on Noel's side and nobody empties the tray (a dry tray, a dust line); the battered copper kettle both use.       F04_C_BATH Cam Ortiz and Noel Price's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Cam Ortiz and Noel Price / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Subway tile walls, hex mosaic floor, plaster ceiling; blown-out flush dome; room washed orange.
      • WC: white bowl and dark wooden seat with lid up; no cistern or flush pipe visible; a small white rectangle on the wall behind.
      • Pedestal sink with brass taps in the corner; cream pleated shower curtain closed as a fluted cylinder.

      Interpretation

      • Sheet-metal ducting in a 1928 tenement bath reads modern; a wall register would read.
      • Same cistern omission as 4A; the WC cannot flush.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Cam Ortiz and Noel Price's is two adults who do not share: two of everything on opposite sides, two towels on separate hooks, a tape line nobody admits to. Two of everything on opposite sides of the basin; two towels on separate hooks; a tape line on the shelf nobody admits to. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      F04 / 4D Transient Guests

      F04_D_BATH the Transient Guests's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: the Transient Guests / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Subway tile walls, hex mosaic floor, blown-out flush dome; room washed orange.
      • Pedestal sink with dark taps; a black switch plate mounted on the tile directly above the sink.
      • WC: bowl with dark wooden seat and lid up; no cistern visible; a short grey stub behind.
      • Cream pleated shower curtain on a curved black rod with rings, hanging to the floor; no tray or tub.
      • Louvered vent box on a square grey duct at the ceiling; khaki door; no mirror or window.
      • Defect: Switch plate on the tile above the sink.
      • Defect: WC has no cistern.
      • Defect: Square duct.
      • Defect: No mirror.

      Interpretation

      • An electric switch in the splash zone of the basin is wrong for any period.
      • Same cistern and duct issues as 4A and 4C.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one the Transient Guests's is a short-let bathroom: hotel-issue soap, one thin towel each, a house-rules card about the bath, nothing of anybody's. Hotel-issue soap, one thin towel each, one of them clearly the building's (wardrobe bible), a rules card about the bath. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      Observed

      • White marble treads, landings and fascia with black iron balusters and wood handrail; several flights visible up the well.

      Interpretation

      • The stair is the one fully period, well-modelled element and carries the public core by itself.
      • The landing outside 5C reads as a service space (bare tan floor, no base), not the public hall it joins.
      • The lift that names the space cannot be read; the yellow strip may be its brass edge but looks like a light leak.

      Narrative

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it. Paint-stiff footprints fade from Iris's door across the landing; the unique piece on this half-landing is a sketch of the light court (she draws it at 13:00). Cores carry sound up and down the building; this is where the Tenant's body is audible.

      F05_WEST_HALL F05 west hall: Nadia and Cal

      The 6.1 m hall with both 5A (F05_DOOR_02) and 5B (F05_DOOR_03) entries / users: Nadia, Cal, Juno on Saturdays, Omar on Tuesdays / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Mahogany wainscot both sides, cream base and plaster above, terrazzo floor; ceiling black.
      • Dark olive unit doors in cream frames at left and right (5A, 5B) with brass knobs; one stands ajar in RV.
      • Door leaves render nearly black; panel outlines barely visible in DT2 and DT3.
      • No ceiling fixture visible; the lamp pool is the only light.
      • DT1 targets F04_B_VESTIBULE_LT_FLUSH_DOME (floor-4 id); tile shows the hall and a door, no fixture.

      • Defect: DT1 station targets a floor-4 fixture id

      Interpretation

      • Finish matches the east hall, so the public standard is consistent; the darkness hides it.
      • The two unit doors are this hall's story and they are unreadable at this exposure.

      Narrative

      A 1912 public corridor under 1928 paint: wainscot to 1.1 m, a dado rail, the picture rail that survived the demolition, enamel floor plates in both cores, a flush dome every few metres and the apartment doors with their transoms. Two very different doors: Nadia's with a measured chalk tick on the floor at the swing's limit and a memo frame beside it; Cal's with an aerial wire run along the dado from the window end to his door (antenna experiments), tacked with insulators. The hall tells both stories. The halls are where neighbours meet and where the building's own voice is loudest: a riser knocks, a door spills light, the lift gate rattles in the shaft.

The exit route is rehearsed. It is also where the building's own hardware shows: the 1912 brass signal outlet beside the later switch plate, the chain guard on the entry door, the painted-over bell push, the Vantry point grille on the ceiling.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Nadia Quell's is a practical single adult: a nail brush, a pumice, carbolic soap, a shaving mirror hung where the light actually falls. A bath with a window; the oxblood lip on a towel edge; a nail brush; the fob of keys on the cabinet knob. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      F05_B_MAIN Cal's listening triangle

      6.35 x 5.75 m, one window, openings to the vestibule and the private hall / users: Cal Dwyer (20:00: he owns no television; the radio is the television) / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak floor, cream plaster, picture rail; pendant with cream shade lit; window with moon; black cast-iron radiator.
      • Round wooden-top table on a white flared tulip pedestal carrying a brown box radio with pale dial, a lead and a black headset.
      • Dark wood side table with a black-cased set, pale dial, and two flat disc cone speakers, brown and cream.
      • Bentwood chairs; a second dark table at the lower left of RV.
      • White subway tile section on the main-room side of the vestibule/bath wall in OV, TH and DT1.
      • Black switch plate by the door; doorways show the lit private hall with a flush dome.
      • No sofa, rug, curtains, aerial wire or shelving of further sets.
      • Defect: Tulip pedestal dining table (1950s form)
      • Defect: Bath wall tiled on the main-room side
      • Defect: Cone speakers render as flat faceted discs

      Interpretation

      • The radio story is legible: a listening set on the table and a bench set with speakers behind it.
      • The tulip pedestal is thirty years late and is the most visible anachronism on the floor.
      • A collector's room should show more sets, parts and wire; this reads as two props.

      Narrative

      The round dining table and chairs, the wireless table with the story radio, headphones and lead, and the domestic radio are installed. The room should be the listening triangle: the chair worn toward the radio (hero object), the reel deck the only warm thing on its own table, and the main set at the third point, with the headphones' lead running across the floor where he dozes; a repair mat on the dining table with a chassis on it (Tuesday's); the tape catalogue on shelves in dated rows, one plain box among them with a courthouse date (proposed; never audible). The decor profile asks for two works separated enough to feel like call and response, not centred. The player infers a man who keeps moments by never letting them end, and whose chair faces the wrong way.

      Proposed backstory

      • The Delayed Voice Reel is a plain box among the dated tapes with a courthouse date.

      F05_B_BATH Cal Dwyer's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Cal Dwyer / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • White subway tile walls, white hex-mosaic floor, flush dome lit; cream door with black switch plate on the tile.
      • Pedestal sink with black taps and trap; dark-framed mirror cabinet above.
      • WC with wooden seat up; undersized white box behind the seat, black flush lever; paper roll holder on the wall.

      Interpretation

      • Period fixtures by type, but the WC cistern is a block and the radiator reads as a ribbed cylinder.
      • No tub leaves the sanitary room half-equipped.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Cal Dwyer's is a single adult's ordinary use: one of everything, a second towel that is really a floorcloth. The bath opens off the vestibule, not the hall: the receiver, cord and battery case coiled on the shelf, the only image of him without it (wardrobe bible). The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      • Icebox, range and trough sink make a convincing 1920s kitchen; the cupboards are the weak objects.
      • The angled icebox reads as deliberate second-hand placement.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it Iris Bell's is paint on the handles, a burner used as a brush-drying rack, a plate with a thumbprint of viridian, a loaf going hard. Paint on the handles, a burner used as a brush-drying rack (brushes bristle-up in a tin on the cold burner), the icebox handle thumbed with viridian; the paint-flecked enamel recipe on this range only. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Iris Bell's is a painter's basin: turpentine jar, brushes bristle-up in a tin, pigment stain in the enamel crazing, a rag on the taps. A painter's basin: turpentine jar, brushes in a tin, pigment stain in the enamel crazing, paint on the taps that never comes off. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      F06_PUBLIC_CORE F06 public core: the top of the stair

      Stair and lift at the top occupied floor; 6C's entry (F06_DOOR_06) opens here; the roof stair continues above / users: all residents, the player, the lift / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Marble-tread stair with black wrought-iron balusters and walnut handrail, continuing upward; white marble landing fascia.
      • TH: dark walnut wainscot panel, a framed wall plaque with illegible lettering, a yellow-lit vertical strip beside the stair.
      • DT1 F06_DOOR_06: cream-painted door, dark recessed upper panel, orange flecked band across the sill, brass fitting top-left.
      • No lift car, gate or indicator identifiable; an iron grille at the top of OV may be the shaft enclosure.
      • Plaster walls plain cream; no ceiling fixture visible, hand lamp is the only light; corners fall to black.
      • Only four tiles captured (OV, RV, TH, DT1).
      • Defect: Lift door or cage not identifiable from any tile
      • Defect: Wall plaque lettering unreadable at capture distance
      • Defect: Orange flecked sill band under F06_DOOR_06 reads as an artefact
      • Defect: No practical fixture visible; lamp-only lighting

      Interpretation

      • The stair reads as a credible 1928 public stair and is the strongest circulation element on the floor.
      • Without a visible lift door the 'passenger lift landing' label is not legible from the frames.
      • The orange sill band is ambiguous (debris, rust or a mat) and recurs under every unit door.

      Narrative

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it. Mae's door opens on the core; the stair continues up to the roof bulkhead, so this core carries roof traffic (Malcolm at dawn, Juno and Sacha at 02:00). Its unique piece: the Vantry prospectus's roof-garden plate, framed, the drawing with people in it. Cores carry sound up and down the building; this is where the Tenant's body is audible.

      F06_SERVICE_HALL F06 service hall (north)

      The 2.4 m maintenance route beside the service core / users: the player, the super, deliveries / coverage: partial

      Observed

      • Narrow corridor, bare tan plaster both sides, flat tan floor, dark flat ceiling with a dropped beam.
      • Doors appear only as thin recessed lines on the left wall; no hardware, frames or thresholds.
      • RV: an open door leaf at the far end with blown-out light beyond; one side door.
      • TH: a small bare box room seen through a doorway whose jambs are blown to pure white.
      • No baseboards, fixtures, pipes or signage; three tiles only.

      • Defect: Doors read as lines without leaves or hardware

      Interpretation

      • Reads as placeholder geometry; a 1928 service corridor should show pipes, a bulb cage, scuffs and a painted dado.
      • Blown jambs suggest an emissive or over-lit material on door frames.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Sacha Reed's is a single adult's ordinary use: one of everything, a second towel that is really a floorcloth. A window bath that doubles as a darkroom rinse: a developing tray in the receptor, a red bulb jar on a nail (unlit), a strap on the hook. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      F06_B_MAIN Jonah's writing room: the sightline

      6.35 x 5.75 m, one window, openings to the vestibule and the private hall / users: Jonah Price (20:00: televised verdicts, in a world with no television; the radio's crime serial) / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Dark wood dining table with stacked cream papers and a mug; bentwood chairs; dark bookcase with books.

      Interpretation

      • The tile panel inside a living room is a material bleed and breaks the plaster story.

      Narrative

      The draft, references, cold coffee, the dining table and chairs, the radio and the plain bookshelf are installed. The decor profile is writer's pauses: words, missing words and one intimate tabletop watercolour; do not fill every silence. The room should turn the dining table into the desk with the task lamp, the draft archive on the shelf in boxes with dates, the wastebasket of rejected endings (hero object) beside it overflowing with crushed sheets, cold-drink rings on every horizontal surface, and the sightline: the alcove door open so the bed sees the desk. The player infers a man who starts books and cannot write the verdict.

      Proposed backstory

      • The rejected endings are all the same chapter.

      • The period kitchen kit reads correctly; the blown dome and grey sink legs are the faults.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an oak icebox with a zinc lining, a drip tray under it that someone has to empty and an ice card in the window. What makes it Jonah Price's is ring stains on every horizontal surface, a wastebasket by the icebox full of paper, cold coffee in three cups, a bread knife in the butter. Three cold coffees, a wastebasket by the icebox full of paper, a bread knife in the butter; the greasy enamel recipe on this range. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Jonah Price's is a single adult's ordinary use: one of everything, a second towel that is really a floorcloth. Off the vestibule: a week's beard in the basin, ink on the towel. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      6.1 x 5.3 m, one window, openings to vestibule, studio and private hall / users: Mae Kessler (20:00: radio drama, letters to dealers); Nadia on Thursdays / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak floor, cream plaster with picture rail, lit pendant, window with a bright moon and a second small bright point.
      • Cream sofa is a boxy untextured block; coffee table a plain wooden box; X-frame side table.
      • Round table on a white tulip pedestal holds a wooden old radio, a stack of cream catalogues and a cluster of small jars.
      • Console with a second radio (three cream dials) and a round cream plate; dark sectional bookshelf with books.
      • Black cast-iron radiator; bentwood chairs; TH shows a flat grey-green pilaster slab.
      • Walls bare; no rug, lamps or pictures; a paper on the floor by the sofa.
      • Defect: Sofa is an untextured modern block
      • Defect: Tulip pedestal table
      • Defect: Coffee table is a plain box
      • Defect: Flat pilaster at the threshold
      • Defect: Bare walls

      Interpretation

      • The appraiser story reads from catalogues, jars and two radios; the sofa and tulip table are mid-century forms.
      • An appraiser's walls with nothing hung is the loudest absence on the floor.

      Narrative

      The sofa, coffee table, round table and chairs, the old radio and oddments and catalogues, the sectional bookshelf and the radio are installed; this is the most furnished of the C-type homes. Decor profile: a provenance cabinet, objects classified on walls, people kept close on furniture, the art not obscured by the archive. The room should hang the classified objects (a row of small framed items with tags), keep the photographs of people on the tables, put the catalogue table at the window with the two cards for one object, and set the tea service for Thursday. The 1912 prospectus on the shelf beside the unopened Estate ledger. The player infers certainty worn as manners, and the one book she has never opened.

      Proposed backstory

      • The Kessler Estate ledger beside the prospectus is never opened.

      F06_C_KITCHEN Mae Kessler's kitchen

      Off the main room through the kitchen opening / users: Mae Kessler / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Oak floor, cream plaster, black switch plate; cream gas range with black top and four burners.
      • Monitor-top electric fridge: cream cabinet, round ridged compressor on top, brass latch (correct for 6C).
      • Sink on flat grey legs with brass faucet; dish rack; black toaster on the base cupboard; white wall cupboard on a tile splash wall.
      • TH: a small dotted sparkle on the open door leaf.
      • Walls otherwise bare; no ceiling fixture seen in OV.
      • Defect: Sink stand flat grey
      • Defect: Oak floor in a kitchen
      • Defect: Dotted sparkle on the door leaf

      Interpretation

      • Correct period kit including the fridge; the grey sink legs and oak floor are the weak notes.

      Narrative

      The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an electric monitor-top on splayed legs, new, expensive, noticeably loud, and the neighbours know who has one. What makes it Mae Kessler's is everything period-correct and nothing after 1935 (which here means nothing after 1927): a Hoosier-type cabinet in order, a covered butter dish, one good knife. One of the four electric flats: the monitor-top she has never replaced, kept pristine (enamel_pristine recipe); a covered butter dish; one good knife. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

      F06_C_BATH Mae Kessler's bathroom

      Private bathroom off the unit's private hall / users: Mae Kessler / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Subway tile walls, hex floor, WC with wooden seat raised and a paper roll on a wall holder.
      • Pedestal sink with brass taps, a small white radiator beside it, a mirror above reflecting tile.
      • Cream pleated shower curtain; cream two-panel door; black switch plate.
      • DT1: a grey rectangular duct runs along the wall near the ceiling with a louvred register and a bracket.
      • Flush dome blown to a white disc; floor specular hotspot; no visible cistern or flush pipe.
      • Defect: Rectangular duct run near the ceiling
      • Defect: Flush dome blown
      • Defect: WC without cistern
      • Defect: Floor hotspot

      Interpretation

      • Best of the three baths for props; the sheet-metal duct run reads modern against 1928 tile.

      Narrative

      Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Mae Kessler's is a single adult who keeps things exact: one toothbrush, one glass, towel squared on the rail, nothing on the floor. Exact and old: a silver-backed brush set, a hair net, the pageboy's pins in a dish; the gloves never come in here. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

      ROOF_PUBLIC_CORE Public roof bulkhead: lift drive and the court skylight

      The public stair's top bulkhead with the guarded lift drive, the pitched light-court skylight beside it and the door onto the west deck / users: all residents, the player, the lift / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Bulkhead interior: landing with iron balustrade and walnut handrail; stair arriving; a dark rectangular hatch in the ceiling.
      • Lift drive in a galvanised bar cage: two grey cable drums, a motor base, a small plate sign inside.
      • A 'ROOF' wall sign with smaller lettering; in RV a second sign's lettering appears mirror-reversed (lift-drive keep-clear text backwards).
      • DT3: the roof public door is a flat dark slab with a brass knob standing on a raised concrete sill block.
      • Plaster walls tan, no fixture visible; lamp only.
      • Defect: Sign text mirror-reversed in RV
      • Defect: Roof door is a flat slab
      • Defect: Cage and drums show no grime or wear
      • Defect: No practical fixture

      Interpretation

      • The drive cage and signs make the space legible; the reversed sign text and the plain slab door are the faults.

      Narrative

      The stair core is the oldest thing the player touches: honed marble treads dished by sixteen years of feet, iron balusters, a rail polished gold at hand height, the enamel floor plate, the lift landing with its brass call plate and the dial above it. The bulkhead holds the Blender lift drive behind its guard and the skylight's pitched panes; it is the one interior on the roof. The skylight is the eye's top (Bible III: it sees from lobby runner to skylight). Cores carry sound up and down the building; this is where the Tenant's body is audible.

      ROOF_DECK_WEST West deck: the tank and three ventilators

      The largest deck (13.45 x 24 m) with the house tank, three ventilator curbs (A, B, C), the west parapet and both passages to the north and south decks / users: the player, Malcolm, Juno, Sacha, Mae / coverage: inspected

      Observed

      • Open deck under a Milky Way sky; flat dark asphalt with faint seams; low brick parapet with pale coping.
      • Timber water tank on four pale legs: body rendered in an orange speckled brick-like texture with two pale hoop bands.
      • Riser pipe from an open brick curb box up to the tank, with a brass ballcock valve and bracket (DT2, DT3).
      • Two ventilator housings read as cream stone plinths with caps; cream bulkhead box with a dark door.
      • DT1 is labelled F06_A_MAIN_LT_PENDANT_SHADE_Semantic and shows the parapet and a standing dark figure silhouette.
      • Neighbouring skyline is flat dark blue blocks with a water tower silhouette and aerial poles.
      • Defect: Tank body textured like brick
      • Defect: Ventilator housings read as plinths
      • Defect: DT1 station mis-targeted to a 6A pendant
      • Defect: Tank legs are flat pale blocks

      Interpretation

      • Tank, riser and ballcock tell the water story; the tank surface says brick, not staves.
      • The fan housings do not read as fans.
      • The silhouette on the far parapet reads as a person; if it is a resident, the roof is occupied at night.

      Narrative

      Open-air maintenance deck over the 1928 membrane: coping, parapets, the four ventilators, the tank on its legs, the chimney, the bulkheads. The tank on its legs is the deck's landmark and the ballcock activity lives at its exposed valve. The three ventilator curbs with their motors sit along the deck; the ILG housings are pending in A06. Malcolm's beds belong here along the west parapet where the morning light comes over it. The roof is where the prospectus drew people in a garden that was a promise; Malcolm keeps that promise alive in beds and communal planters, and the schedules put four residents up here on different nights.
